headline: Breakwall Porgies Stacked, Blackfish Sulking, Sea Bass Filling the Gaps
subhead: The rockpiles are still paying dividends on scup and sea bass while the tautog take a summer siesta and stripers slide into the shadows.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, half-tide push, I'm working the outer breakwall off New Haven Harbor with a high-low rig and green crab chunks, and I can't get the bait down twenty feet before something's chewing. Porgies — scup, if you want to be proper about it — stacked on the rockpile in 18 to 22 feet like they're waiting in line. Nothing huge, mostly 9 to 11 inches, but enough 12-plus fish mixed in to make the cooler heavy by the time the tide slowed. That's the story on this beat right now: the bottom bite is doing the heavy lifting while the water upstairs sorts itself out.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on most of these rockpiles, which is normal for late July but the size has been a pleasant surprise. I've had a handful of 14 to 16-inch fish come off the deeper humps around Falkner Island — 30 to 35 feet, drifting squid strips and small Gulp baits on a jig head — and one gentleman on the dock had a fish pushing three pounds off Stratford Shoal that made his day. The keepers aren't wall-to-wall, but if you're working structure with any kind of intent — moving spot to spot instead of anchoring on one rock and hoping — you're putting fish in the box.

Blackfish, on the other hand, are being difficult. This is typical mid-summer behavior — tautog don't love warm water any more than we love fishing in it — and the bite has gone quiet on the shallower rockpiles around the harbor mouth. I found a few willing fish early, right at first light before the boat traffic stirred things up, working green crabs tight to the mussel beds on the Milford Gulf side. But it's a grind right now. If blackfish is your target, I'd fish the first hour of daylight and not much past it, then pivot to porgies and sea bass for the rest of the trip.

Stripers are exactly where you'd expect them with the water running warm — Kings Point was reading 72 and change this week, and while I don't have a hard number for the harbor itself, it's tracking right there with it. That kind of warmth pushes keeper bass into a low-light and after-dark pattern, and Charles Island is proving it out. The sandbar that connects to the island at low tide has been holding fish on the ebb right at dusk — live eels and chunk bunker fished tight to the drop-off edge, right where the current starts to rip off the bar. Daytime, forget it; those fish are sulking deep or tucked into shadow. If you want a shot at a keeper on this beat right now, plan your trip around the last hour of light into full dark, and fish the moving water, not the slack.

Bluefish have been a nice surprise on top of Stratford Shoal in the early morning — nothing like the blitzes you're hearing about further down the coast on the bunker schools, but enough choppers slashing through peanut bunker at dawn to make topwater fun again. Deadly Dicks and small poppers worked fast across the surface have been drawing strikes. It's a short window, usually the first 45 minutes of light before the sun gets up and the fish drop, but it's been consistent enough this week that I'd call it worth setting an alarm for.

Fluke are still the most dependable bite in the zone if you're willing to move and cover structure edges. Milford Gulf and the drop-offs around the Charles Island sandbar have both produced fish in the 3 to 5 pound range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktail combos, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the incoming. The key word is moving water — fluke here want current, and we're heading into a first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the push through the middle of the week. That's not a death sentence, but it means shorter, weaker bite windows around the tide changes. I'd fish the top of the flood and the top of the ebb rather than trying to grind it out mid-tide when the water's barely crawling.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason to change the game plan much. The rockpile bite on porgies and sea bass should hold steady through the neap — that bottom bite doesn't need much current to stay productive, which is exactly why it's carrying the week. Blackfish should start perking back up once we get past this stretch of flat calm heat, probably late next week if a cold front pushes through and knocks the surface temp down a couple degrees. Stripers will stay a dawn-dusk-and-dark proposition until that happens too. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be on the breakwall at first light for blues and porgies, then off to Charles Island for the last of the outgoing tide before the sun climbs too high. That's about as honest a plan as I can give you right now — the water's warm, the current's about to go soft, and the fish are telling us to work smarter, not longer.
